summary.title: Evolutionary Database Design
summary.one_liner: Learn how to change a production database's schema and data safely over time by treating every change as a small, version-controlled migration script applied through CI.
keywords: split a column into multiple columns example
takeaways: Represent every schema and data change as a small, sequentially numbered migration script stored in version control with application code.
Give each developer a private database instance (schema or local VM) so experiments do not disturb shared work, and rebuild them regularly.
Integrate database changes into mainline frequently (at least daily) so CI runs migrations and tests against a copy of the database.
Never alter schemas with GUI tools or ad hoc DDL; track applied migrations with a changelog table, as tools like Flyway do.
Work closely with DBAs, who review migrations and help with significant schema changes.
summary.summary: The article, by Martin Fowler and Thoughtworks colleagues, describes techniques for evolving a database's schema and contents alongside agile application development. It walks through a worked example where a developer splits an inventory code column into three new columns using a migration script, updating application code, views and indexes together. It then lays out core practices: close DBA collaboration, putting all database artifacts in version control, treating every change as a numbered migration tracked by a changelog table, giving each developer a private database, and integrating through continuous integration and a deployment pipeline. The page also notes limitations, such as heavily customized multi-schema deployments.
technologies: Continuous Integration servers (GoCD, Jenkins, Bamboo, Travis CI, Snap CI)
